content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies a supervised learning algorithm for trees based on the kernel density estimator. The proposed method is formulated as the fuzzy decision tree (FDT). An efficient algorithm of finding the splitting point is theoretically justified. Numerical experiments using standard datasets are conducted to show the proposed method's effectiveness compared to existing tree-based learning algorithms.
content.main_review:
This paper is clearly written. A theoretical justification provided in Theorem 1 is interesting. However, the authors did not provide theoretical insight on statistical properties, such as the robustness of the proposed method. In Section 3.3.1, KDDT is formulated as an FDT with the specified splitting function. Based on such a result, The authors could investigate more detailed statistical properties of the KDDT.

In numerical experiments, the standard datasets for multiclass classification problems were used. In addition to that experiment, showing the robustness properties against contaminated data would be nice.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, This paper is clearly written. However, theoretical insight and numerical experiments were not enough to justify the usefulness of the proposed method.

content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback. If by robustness, you mean adversarial robustness as we have mentioned in the paper, we believe that the theoretical inclination to greater robustness is intuitive, as any perturbation of a data point within the bandwidth of its kernel is considered during fitting. Nonetheless, we do not claim that this certainly improves adversarial robustness, but only briefly mention it in the discussion as a behavior we expect to see and will study in future work.

As mentioned in the discussion, we cannot currently give a complete robustness analysis because there does not yet exist a verification methodology for KDDTs. We are working on one and plan to do this analysis in a future work.

If there are other concerns, we would appreciate the feedback. Please also see our general response to the reviews, which summarizes revisions.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3468 by Reviewer aDpD

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a weighted approach to improve the performance of a decision tree predictor by smoothing over the tree via a kernel approach. The idea is as follows. Given a decision tree, a usual predictor conduct prediction based on the average of response $Y$ of those observation whose covariates belong to the same leaf/node/region of the tree. The proposed approach replace this local average by a weighted average where the weights are constructed by the smoothing kernel. And the final prediction is another layer of weighted average of the new local average. The authors provide an analysis of the computation complexity and describe the a simple way to compute the final estimate. Empirical analysis on benchmark datasets show the improvement of the proposed approach.
content.main_review:
While this paper introduced a novel approach for predictions, it seems to me that some key analysis was not conducted so it is hard to gain insight from the proposed method. Here are my main comments on this paper.

1. Improving the description of the method.
This paper introduced the tree predictor from a graph perspective and apply a smoothing. If I understand it correctly, the procedure can be equivalently written as follows: 
Given a decision tree, the leaves form a partition of the feature space $R_1,\cdots, R_K$, where $K$ is the total number of leaves. 
For each observation $(Y_i,X_i)$, in the classical method, the value of response $Y_i$ only contribute to a region $R_j$ based on which region/leaf that $X_i$ belongs to. 
The proposed method 'smooth' out this procedure by applying a smoothing kernel at $X_i$ so that there are some chances that $X_i'$ (after smoothed) may belong to other leaves (generally nearby leaves). 
The conditional mean of leave/region $R_j$, $v_j= E(Y|X\in R_j)$, is then replaced by a weighted average of $Y_i$ according to the above chance. 
The final predictor is a weighted average of the conditional mean and the weight is again derived from the above probability.
I would recommend adding alternative description of the method to the paper. This may draw new insights in to the method and may help the readers to understand the method better. 

2. Re-structure Section 3.1 and 3.2. 
I think some contents in Section 3.1 and 3.2 should be restructured. 
(i) At the beginning of Section 3.1, the authors should emphasized that we are assuming the tree is given and the paths refer to the root-leave path.
(ii) The prediction $\hat y_{\hat f}(x)$ in Sec 3.1 involves the concepts of $v^{(\ell)}$ but $v^{(\ell)}$ was later introduced in Sec 3.2. 

3. Justification of the smoothing. 
The key novelty of the proposed method is the use of a smoothing kernel to the tree predictor. But the authors did not provide any argument on why this is a preferred approach. Some argument or analysis should be done to justify this procedure.
In particular, why is the weighted estimator of $\hat y_{\hat f}(x)$ in Sect. 3.1 is preferred over the usual tree predictor?
The usual conditional mean has a simple justification that it is the minimizer of the MSE. But when we add weights to it, the resulting predictor will not be optimal under MSE. So it was not clear why this weighted approach is preferred.


4. Justification of the weighted estimator $v^{(\ell)}.$
In Sec. 3.2, the authors recommend using a weighted estimator of the conditional mean. But why is this weighted conditional mean a better estimator than the usual conditional mean estimator (without smoothing, it is just simple sample average within the leave/region)?
The usual tree method has already done a smoothing based on the region of leaves (so any point $x$ in the same leave will contribute the same to the prediction). Adding an additional layer of smoothing seems to be redundant and could introduce additional bias.


5. The power of product kernel. 
To me, the idea of using a product kernel shows a benefits of computation in the current paper. The authors may want to highlight this contribution. There are other smoothing kernels (such as radial basis kernel) for multivariate features but they may not have the same computational benefits as the product kernel.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while this paper has some novelty in the combining of a smoothing kernel and tree predictor, a couple of key analysis is missing in the paper. It was not very clear to me why the weighted approach should be a preferred approach. The use of tree itself has already introduced the concept of smoothing, so adding another layer of kernel smoothing may introduce more bias in the output.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3468 by Reviewer jz39

content.summary_of_the_paper: The given paper proposes a decision tree model which incorporates kernel density estimation (KDE) and the corresponding learning algorithm. Specifically, KDE is used to assign a weight (probability) for each root-to-leaf path and the final prediction is obtained by the weighted sum of all (or a subset of) leaves. Although authors emphasize that their method is a generalization of "fuzzy decision trees", the term "fuzzy" here is a bit confusing as the most commonly accepted name for such trees is soft decision tree.
content.main_review:
I will break my score justification to the following categories:

1. Novelty
Incorporating KDE into decision trees by itself is not a novel idea. As it was mentioned by authors, such a model has been studied in Smyth (1995), Itani (2020), etc. In general, the method conceptually reminds soft decision trees: each root-to-leaf path is assigned a non-negative weight (probability), each leaf's output is multiplied by that leaf and averaged. Here, the only modification is that not all leaves might be employed (depending on bandwidth). In terms of training, the approach is the same as in CART (top-down tree induction based on purity criterion) but with kernel function taken into account. The proposed efficient optimal splitting algorithm is based on sorting and clever traversal over intervals but a similar approach is already used in the original CART book by Breiman.

2. Experiments
Authors provide a comparison against CART trees (both in single tree or ensemble setting) which is clearly very simple baseline. Even in that case, the differences in RF and ExtraTrees columns are not statistically significant. This might be due to simplicity of the given datasets. In that case, I'd suggest authors to perform evaluations on somewhat larger benchmarks (e.g. original XGBoost paper uses Higgs dataset with ~10M instances). Next, the most important missing baseline is the soft DTs as they are closely related to the proposed model. I encourage to use one or several soft tree based approaches (e.g. [1]) as related baselines. Moreover, DT research is not restricted with CART or "fuzzy" decision trees. You may want to compare against more advanced tree learning methods that are "non-greedy" and generally outperform CART-style algorithms: optimal decision trees [2,3], alternating optimization of decision trees [4], etc. [5]. By the way, some of them can be included into the related work section.

[1] Nicholas Frosst, Geoffrey Hinton. Distilling a Neural Network Into a Soft Decision Tree. https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.09784

[2] Dimitris Bertsimas, Jack Dunn. Optimal classification trees. https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/110328

[3] Jimmy Lin, Chudi Zhong, Diane Hu, Cynthia Rudin, Margo Seltzer. Generalized and Scalable Optimal Sparse Decision Trees. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08690

[4] Arman Zharmagambetov, Miguel Carreira-Perpinan. Smaller, more accurate regression forests using tree alternating optimization. http://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/zharmagambetov20a.html

[5] Norouzi et al. Efficient non-greedy optimization of decision trees. https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.04056

Other comments/questions:
- Equations are not numbered which makes them hard to refer during review. The 2nd set of equations in p.4 starts from equality sign which is confusing. Does it equal to the above equation (which cannot be true since that eq. is defined for 1 attribute only) or just u^l? The relation of that equation with the 3rd equation in the same page (upper and lower bounds) are not well described. 

- Interpretability. Abstract and conclusion emphasize interpretability of the proposed model. However, this claim was not supported by experiments or by any other evidences. I'd encourage authors to re-consider this claim (or provide evidences) as I believe that the obtained trees are not trivially interpretable. Because, first of all, traditional CART trees by itself may be hard to interpret if the resulting trees are big (and deep). The proposed trees are also axis-aligned (one feature at a node) which tend to grow deep, especially with modern large-scale datasets. On top of that, there are multiple paths are possible which requires inspecting all of them. Second, according to the experiments, a true improvement comes by ensembling trees into a forest in which case the story about interpretability becomes more tricky.

- I didn't quite get how bandwidth is used with traditional trees (i.e., no kernels). From my understanding, applying kernel there is equivalent to feature/threshold rescaling?

- Did you report somewhere the runtime of the efficient optimal splitting vs simple enumeration? What was the avg speedup?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper definitely carries some interesting ideas: more powerful tree model which leverages KDE; fast learning algorithm to train them which asymptotically improve over enumeration; using a subset of paths which is controlled by bandwidth, etc. However, I am leaning towards rejection of this paper due to shortcomings in experiments and methodological novelty (as described in the main review).

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3468 by Reviewer jz39

content.title: Reply from the authors
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed feedback. We have revised certain parts of the manuscript to better clarify some items, and we would like to address the points you have put forth. Please also see our general response to the reviews, which summarizes revisions.

We are aware that tree models using multiple decision paths have gone by multiple names. We acknowledge in the introduction that works use various names, including soft decision trees, but that for the purpose of this paper we use "fuzzy decision trees" as an umbrella term. This is because we have seen this name appearing most often in the most relevant works, particularly those using greedy construction with feature-aligned splitting. We have also added a note of the alternative names in the abstract.

1. We are not claiming novelty either for the idea of using KDE with decision trees, nor for the idea of fuzzy/soft decision trees. The novelty is the way we use KDE with decision trees, which is different from the related works and intentionally does not stray far from the conventional decision tree paradigm. Moreover, this alters the usual fuzzy/soft decision tree formulation by introducing a dependence between splitting functions across layers unlike any existing work we are aware of, which makes it compatible with the kernel interpretation. We have also acknowledged that the fitting algorithm is based on CART, but it has innovations to efficiently extend to the fuzzy/soft tree formalism, and we provide accompanying proofs of optimality in its choice of splits, another feat we are unaware of for greedy splitting of continuous features in fuzzy/soft trees. We have modified the text of the introduction to attempt to better clarify these points.

2. We have run the experiments again for the revision with 10-fold cross-validation rather than a single train-test split, and the results appear to reflect our claims more consistently. Moreover, we compare in the arena of CART-based models because they are most related to our model and share similar utility. These models may not be the best in every setting, but they generally do very well, if not the best, on many tabular datasets, and are used widely in real applications even today. Therefore we believe we are justified in claiming that our models, by improving and adding utility in this area, are useful.
We are aware of and mention globally optimizing fuzzy/soft trees in the introduction, but believe they are out of scope to go into detail for this work.

- We have attempted to clarify the equations to address the stated concerns.
- In the revision we have made sure that our claims are only that our models, without prediction kernels, are interpreted in the same way as conventional trees, and that with prediction kernels, the kernel formalism may aid interpretation (as the prediction is simply the expectation of the tree's prediction over the kernel). We mention that conventional trees are "often considered to be interpretable to humans," which we believe is fair.
- Using a fitting kernel, but not a prediction kernel, is not equivalent to feature and threshold rescaling. Perhaps the most concrete way to describe it is that it is equivalent to performing KDE with the fitting kernel, sampling infinitely many points from the density estimate, then fitting a tree to those points using CART. We have made efforts to better explain the concept of the fitting kernel on a high level in the text, including a figure that illustrates how it can result in an entirely different choice of splits.
- If by simple enumeration, you mean choosing candidate thresholds and fully evaluating the split at each, we mentioned briefly that there is a linear cost in the size of the data for each candidate. In the revised version, we have further clarified this, particularly that if all candidates are evaluted in this way, the total cost is quadratic in the number of data samples. Moreover, without our Theorem 1, we are not aware of a way to identify candidate thresholds, one of which is optimal, in the fuzzy tree setting.

content.title: Revision notes
content.comment:
Thanks to the reviewers for your feedback. We have submitted a revision to improve the paper and address your concerns in what ways we can given the time constraints and page limit. We have also responded to your individual reviews. There were a few common misunderstandings about the methodology, so we encourage you to read our replies and consider our efforts to improve communication in the manuscript.

The main changes in the revision are:
 - A reorganization of Section 3 according to feedback.
 - An attempt to more thoroughly describe the methods at a high level, especially in Section 3, as well as a new figure to give an illustrative example.
 - A re-run of the experiments using 10-fold cross-validation instead of a single train-test split to reduce the variance of the computed accuracies. We also used ensembles for bandwidth selection for ensembles instead of trees; we found that the previous strategy can result in too large a bandwidth for ensembles. This resulted in clearer gains for random forests, but it is not clear that there are gains for ExtraTrees. With these changes, the bandwidth selection using leave-one-out cross-validation of the KDE-only loss was only the best performer on one dataset, so we removed it from the results to simplify presentation.
 - A clear statement of the novel contributions in the introduction.
 - Moving the algorithms to the appendix to satisfy page limits with the additional content.
